lesson.title: Max läuft weg
lesson.subtitle: A present-tense story: a dog, an open door, and a happy ending
lesson.label: s1

hook.title: Before You Read
hook.content: This is a short story in the present tense, so everything happens in front of you. Follow three things: the dog Max, the open door, and how Paul feels. Read it once for the story, then once for the words you already know. You do not need every word to understand what happens.

footnotes.title: Bellen
footnotes.content: das Bellen = barking. It appears in the story as a sound, not as a new grammar rule. You can hear it and keep reading.

footnotes.title: überall
footnotes.content: überall = everywhere. It is the picture-word for Paul's search: in the garden, in the house, everywhere.

footnotes.title: spielen
footnotes.content: spielen = to play. Jeden Morgen spielen Paul und Max im Garten = every morning Paul and Max play in the garden.

pattern.title: Die Geschichte
pattern.content:
Paul hat einen Hund. Sein Hund heißt Max. Max ist klein, braun und sehr schnell.

Jeden Morgen spielen Paul und Max im Garten. Aber heute ist die Tür offen. Max läuft in die Stadt. Paul sucht Max überall. Er geht in den Garten und in das Haus. Max ist nicht da. Paul ist traurig.

Dann hört Paul ein lautes Bellen. Max kommt zu Paul. Paul lacht und sagt: „Max! Du bist wieder da!“

Am Abend sind Paul und Max müde. Sie schlafen im Haus.

exercises.prompt: Reading check — match each story sentence with its English meaning:

matching_pairs.english: Max is small, brown, and very fast.
matching_pairs.german: Max ist klein, braun und sehr schnell.

matching_pairs.english: In the evening Paul and Max are tired.
matching_pairs.german: Am Abend sind Paul und Max müde.

exercises.target_answer: Paul hat einen Hund., Max ist klein, braun und sehr schnell., Heute ist die Tür offen., Max läuft in die Stadt., Paul sucht Max überall., Am Abend sind Paul und Max müde.
exercises.meaning: the story beats: Paul, Max, the open door, the search, the happy ending
exercises.explanation: Six sentences carry the whole plot. If you can re-tell these six beats, you have read the story.

exercises.prompt: Why does Paul search for Max?
options: Because Max runs into the city.
Because Paul wants to buy bread.
exercises.target_answer: Because Max runs into the city.
exercises.meaning: Max leaves through the open door, so Paul goes looking for him.
exercises.explanation: The cause is the open door: Max läuft in die Stadt. Paul's search is the result, not the cause.

exercises.prompt: Where does Paul look for Max?
options: In the garden and in the house
In the city and at the station
In the kitchen and in the garden
At the market and in the house
exercises.target_answer: In the garden and in the house
exercises.meaning: Paul searches the garden and the house before Max comes back.
exercises.explanation: The text says: Er geht in den Garten und in das Haus. Those are the two places he checks.

exercises.prompt: How does Paul feel before Max comes back?
exercises.meaning: Paul is sad while Max is missing.
exercises.explanation: The sentence Paul ist traurig gives the feeling directly; then Max comes back and Paul laughs.

exercises.prompt: Rebuild the sentence: 'Max comes back to Paul.'
exercises.explanation: German puts the destination after the verb: Max kommt zu Paul. The extra chips are there to make you choose the right ending.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the last scene: 'The dog runs quickly home.'
twist.target_answer: Der Hund läuft schnell nach Hause
twist.explanation: nach Hause is the fixed phrase for 'home' (direction). Keep the verb in second position and the direction at the end: Der Hund läuft schnell nach Hause.

summary.outcome: Read a short present-tense story and answer who, where, and how questions.

use_example.german: Max läuft in die Stadt. Paul sucht ihn überall.
use_example.english: Max runs into the city. Paul searches for him everywhere.

summary.takeaway: A story is a chain of small sentences: who does what, where it happens, and how it ends. You do not need every word to follow the chain.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: a lost puppy, a kind girl, and an old man on a bench.

hund.context_phrase: Der Hund schläft auf dem Sofa.
hund.context_translation: The dog sleeps on the sofa.
hund.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hundaz — cognate with English hound, the same ancient dog-word. [wiktionary]

stadt.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *stadiz — the twin of stead (homestead, instead); final d devoiced to [t]. [wiktionary]

laufen.context_phrase: Ich laufe jeden Morgen im Park.
laufen.context_translation: I run every morning in the park.
laufen.etymology_derivation: Class 7 strong verb from Proto-West Germanic *hlaupan - the exact relative of English leap and lope; läuft-lief-gelaufen preserves the old ablaut. [wiktionary]

schnell.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German snel, Proto-Germanic *snellaz, meaning quick and bold; the exact English cognate is the rare word snell, still heard in northern England and Scotland. [wiktionary]

klein.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *klainiz 'clean, fine' — the TRUE twin of English clean; the meaning drifted from 'clean' to 'small'. [wiktionary]

braun.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *brūn — English brown is the same Germanic word. [wiktionary]

müde.context_phrase: Ich bin müde und gehe ins Bett.
müde.context_translation: I am tired and go to bed.
müde.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *mōþī; only Dutch moe named — no English cognate, memorize this one. [wiktionary]

abend.context_phrase: Am Abend lese ich ein Buch.
abend.context_translation: In the evening I read a book.
abend.etymology_derivation: The twin of archaic English even/eve ('evening') — the same *ēbandaz root; Guten Abend keeps the wish-accusative. [wiktionary]

garten.context_translation: The children play in the garden.

tür.etymology_derivation: d → t with vowel mutation to ü.

offen.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *opan — English open is listed among cognates, kin to auf. [wiktionary]

suchen.context_translation: I am looking for my glasses.
suchen.etymology_derivation: k → ch. Direct transitive object without prepositions.

finden.context_translation: I cannot find it / I find it not.
finden.etymology_derivation: Stem find + infinitive -en (German keeps pure short [ɪ] vowel).

traurig.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *dreuzagaz — English dreary is the cognate, with English d ↔ German t. [wiktionary]

hören.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German hœren, from Old High German hōren. English hear is a listed cognate. [wiktionary]

wieder.context_translation: We will see each other again.
wieder.etymology_derivation: Old High German widar 'against', from West Germanic *wiþr 'toward, against' — the page names English wither and widdershins as cognates; German wieder turned against into again. [wiktionary]

laut.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *hlūd; only Old Saxon hlūd compared — the loud link is not on the page. [wiktionary]

nacht.context_phrase: In der Nacht ist es hier sehr ruhig.
nacht.context_translation: At night it is very quiet here.

bett.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *badją — explicitly cognate with English bed; the High German d→t gives the final -tt. [wiktionary]

haus.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hūsą — an exact twin of English house, down to the diphthong. [wiktionary]
